name: Teriparatide

lead: Teriparatide is a recombinant fragment of human parathyroid hormone (residues 1-34) used as a daily injection to treat severe osteoporosis. Unlike most osteoporosis drugs, which slow bone loss, it stimulates new bone formation.

It appears in looksmaxxing talk because of speculation that bone-building drugs could enhance jaw or facial bone. No evidence has been published for cosmetic skeletal change in healthy adults, and its approval covers osteoporosis only.

paras: Intermittent exposure to PTH fragments stimulates osteoblasts through the PTH1 receptor, increasing bone formation more than resorption in the short term. Continuous exposure instead promotes bone breakdown, which is why the treatment pattern matters. Effects are largest in trabecular bone such as the spine.

Possible effects include nausea, dizziness, leg cramps and raised blood calcium. Osteosarcoma was seen in high-dose rodent studies, which led to a former boxed warning and treatment duration limits. It is prescription-only, costly and not recommended for people with certain bone conditions or prior radiation. It is not approved as a cosmetic treatment, and no evidence supports cosmetic use.

lead: Teriparatide is a recombinant form of the first 34 amino acids of human parathyroid hormone (PTH 1-34), the portion that activates the PTH1 receptor [1][2]. It is a prescription bone-anabolic drug given by daily subcutaneous injection to treat osteoporosis, and was first marketed by Eli Lilly as Forteo [1][3]. Unlike most osteoporosis drugs, which slow bone breakdown, it stimulates new bone formation [1].

Its approved uses are postmenopausal women with osteoporosis at high fracture risk, men with primary or hypogonadal osteoporosis, and men and women with glucocorticoid-associated osteoporosis [1][3][2]. Randomised trials show it reduces vertebral fractures, and in a head-to-head trial it outperformed an oral bisphosphonate on new fractures in women with severe osteoporosis [4][3].

Teriparatide appears in some looksmaxxing and bodybuilding forum discussion as one of several substances speculated to promote bone formation. No published study has tested it for cosmetic skeletal or facial-bone change in healthy adults, and its regulatory approvals cover osteoporosis only.
infobox: Forteo, Forsteo, Bonsity, Qutavina, Livogiva, Osnuvo and others [1]
FDA approval November 2002 (Forteo); EU authorisation June 2003 [1][3]
FDA removed the boxed osteosarcoma warning in November 2020 [3]

paras: The US label lists treatment of postmenopausal women with osteoporosis at high risk of fracture (a prior osteoporotic fracture, multiple risk factors, or failure of or intolerance to other therapy), increasing bone mass in men with primary or hypogonadal osteoporosis at high risk, and osteoporosis associated with sustained systemic glucocorticoid therapy [2][1]. Clinical overviews position anabolic agents such as teriparatide, abaloparatide and romosozumab for people at especially high near-term fracture risk, such as those with very low bone density or previous vertebral or hip fractures [5][6].

Treatment has typically been limited to a lifetime maximum of about two years, after which an antiresorptive drug is generally recommended to preserve gains in bone density [3]. Off-label use has been explored in other skeletal conditions, including osteogenesis imperfecta, and in fracture healing, for which small registered trials exist [3][7].

There is no approved cosmetic use. Some forum members have raised the idea that bone-forming substances might thicken or enlarge bones, mostly in discussion of bone size for physique or frame, but no published research has examined teriparatide for jaw, facial or other cosmetic bone change in healthy adults.

The pivotal Fracture Prevention Trial in postmenopausal women with osteoporosis reportedly found that about 21 months of daily teriparatide lowered new vertebral fractures by roughly 65 percent and nonvertebral fragility fractures by roughly 53 percent versus placebo [3]. Wikipedia describes about an 8 percent spinal bone-density increase after one year and a reduced risk of hip fracture, with no reduction in forearm or wrist fracture [1]. In the VERO trial, teriparatide produced fewer new vertebral fractures than the bisphosphonate risedronate in women with severe osteoporosis [4]. A network meta-analysis prepared for the American College of Physicians evaluated fracture-prevention treatments for low bone mass and osteoporosis, including anabolic agents [8].

The DATA trial found that combining teriparatide with denosumab increased bone mineral density more than either drug alone, and its switch extension examined transitions between the two agents [9][10]. Wikipedia notes that switching from denosumab to teriparatide has been associated with progressive or transient bone loss [1]. In the glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis setting, a trial compared teriparatide with alendronate [11]. Reviews also compare teriparatide with abaloparatide, a PTHrP analogue, and with romosozumab [5][12][13][14].
Clinical research on teriparatide is extensive but concerns osteoporosis, fracture healing and related bone disease, not appearance.

Randomised trials include the Fracture Prevention Trial against placebo [3], the VERO trial against risedronate in severe osteoporosis [4], the DATA and DATA-Switch trials combining or sequencing teriparatide with denosumab [9][10], a comparison with alendronate in glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis [11], and a phase 2 study of an oral PTH(1-34) tablet in postmenopausal women [15]. A related PTHrP analogue, abaloparatide, was tested against placebo for vertebral fractures in the ACTIVE trial [13], and romosozumab was tested in a phase 2 trial in postmenopausal women with low bone density [14].

Registered trials include comparisons of biosimilar or reformulated teriparatide products with Forteo in patients and healthy volunteers, a microneedle-patch PTH dose-ranging study, an imaging study of bone structure, a trial in ankle fractures, and a nasal-spray study [16][17][18][19][20][21][7][22]. Reviews describe the effects of teriparatide, abaloparatide and romosozumab in postmenopausal osteoporosis [5], and general osteoporosis overviews place anabolic therapy in clinical context [23][6][24][25].

Common reactions listed on the US label include arthralgia, pain and nausea; other effects reported in clinical use include headache, dizziness, leg cramps, orthostatic hypotension and raised blood calcium [2][1][3]. The label also describes hypersensitivity reactions, hypercalcaemia and skin calcification, urolithiasis and a risk of digoxin toxicity [2].

Osteosarcoma developed in rats given high doses for much of their lifetime, which led to a boxed warning and limits on treatment duration; human surveillance has not demonstrated an increased risk, and the FDA removed the boxed warning in November 2020 [1][3]. The label still advises avoiding use in people at increased baseline risk of osteosarcoma, such as those with Paget's disease of bone, prior skeletal radiation therapy, open growth plates, bone metastases or a history of skeletal malignancy [2][1]. There are no adequate data in pregnant women, and the label recommends considering discontinuation when pregnancy is recognised [2].

Endogenous 84-amino-acid PTH is the primary regulator of calcium and phosphate metabolism in bone and kidney, and teriparatide and the 34 N-terminal residues bind the same receptors with the same affinity [2]. Sustained high PTH increases bone resorption and depletes bone, whereas intermittent exposure, as with once-daily injection, activates osteoblasts more than osteoclasts and so produces net bone formation [1]. Laboratory work on osteoclast-like cell formation and its regulation by hormones underlies understanding of how PTH acts in bone [26]. The effect is largest in trabecular (spongy) bone such as the vertebrae [3].

Teriparatide is identical in sequence to the first 34 amino acids of human PTH and is produced by recombinant DNA technology [1][2]. Abaloparatide is a related analogue of PTH-related peptide with a different binding profile at the receptor [12].

Teriparatide was approved for medical use in the United States in 1987, according to Wikipedia, and the FDA approved Forteo for osteoporosis in men and postmenopausal women at high fracture risk on 26 November 2002; EU authorisation followed in June 2003 [1][3]. A recombinant product (Bonsity) was approved in October 2019, and European biosimilars (Qutavina and Livogiva) in 2020, with Canada approving Osnuvo in January 2020 [1]. The FDA removed the osteosarcoma boxed warning in November 2020 [3].
Teriparatide is available only by prescription. Brand and biosimilar names include Forteo, Forsteo, Bonsity, Qutavina, Livogiva and Osnuvo [1].

Community mentions are sparse. A 2013 T Nation thread on bone size lists teriparatide, with growth hormone, vitamin D and calcitonin, among substances said to contribute to bone formation, in the context of whether bones can be thickened [27]. Another thread notes the Wikipedia teriparatide page in a discussion of bone health in low testosterone [28]. Within these discussions the drug is generally raised as a treatment for bone loss rather than as an established cosmetic tool.

lore.intro: Teriparatide is mentioned only occasionally on forums, usually as a bone-health drug in testosterone and hormone threads and, in a few posts, as a substance said to contribute to bone formation [27][28].
